The Treasury is currently managing pressures from rising government borrowing costs, public finance constraints, and higher defense spending needs ahead of the October 28 Budget.
Conservative critics and other political opponents argue that Healey's plans and funding announcements do enough to address increasing debt and economic worries.

title: Hundreds of far-right protesters descend on Portsmouth after small boat arrival
author: Diane Taylor; Charlie Moloney
content:
Hundreds of far-right activists have descended on Portsmouth, where a small boat with 140 asylum seekers on board was intercepted heading towards the Portsmouth coast. It sparked a major response with a helicopter, an aeroplane and lifeboats sent to the scene. It is thought to be the first time such a large boat containing asylum seekers has been brought to Portsmouth and the first time a large group of anti-migrant protesters have tried to block newly arrived asylum seekers from being processed.
The boat’s occupants have been brought to shore in the maritime city and the Home Office’s plan is to take them to Manston, outside Ramsgate in Kent, where small boat arrivals are processed.
Videos circulating on social media show large groups of protesters close to where coaches of newly arrived asylum seekers are parked. The protesters in Portsmouth were blocking the coaches carrying asylum seekers from leaving.
Hampshire police urged people to avoid the area, and said a dispersal order was in place.
The government has condemned what it described as the “thuggish behaviour” of the protesters. “We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we are seeing tonight,” a government spokesperson said. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.”
![Boats carrying migrants, one of them at the port with passengers disembarking](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a89277134f48ff84d91d8843437283df13891b43/0_0_7113_4878/master/7113.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In a livestream from the scene, Daniel Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo – a former bodyguard of the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon – encouraged viewers to travel to Portsmouth to join the protest.
Thomas has recently established Patriot Platform which blocked part of port of Dover on Saturday. He previously launched Operation Overlord which planned to send far-right activists to France to “stop the boats”. He and his supporters filmed themselves slashing abandoned dinghies on a French beach. The french authorities subsequently banned him from France.
Small boat crossings so far this year have reduced by more than 40% compared with the same period last year. While the Home Office has disrupted the smugglers’ business model, their methods appear to have evolved by launching boats such as the one that arrived on Sunday evening from different parts of the coast, much further from the UK, making the crossings more dangerous.
Most small boat arrivals are rescued by Border Force and RNLI boats on the English side of the Channel and brought ashore in Dover.
A Maritime and Coastguard Agency spokesperson said: “In response to a report on 6 September of a small boat heading towards the Hampshire coast, HM Coastguard sent lifeboats, an HM Coastguard helicopter, an HM Coastguard aeroplane and HM Coastguard Rescue Teams.
“Border Force, Border Security Command, Hampshire police and south central ambulance service were also sent.”
Stand Up To Racism posted on X: “another attempt by fascist Danny Tommo to whip up pogroms against refugees.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border. Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election.
“We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020.
“But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches.”
summary: Hundreds of far-right protesters gathered in Portsmouth to block coaches carrying 140 asylum seekers who arrived on a small boat. The government condemned the demonstrators' intimidating behaviour, while Hampshire police issued a dispersal order and urged people to avoid the area. The asylum seekers were brought ashore to be processed and transferred to Manston in Kent.
key_points: A small boat carrying 140 asylum seekers was intercepted heading toward Portsmouth.
Far-right protesters attempted to block coaches carrying the newly arrived asylum seekers from leaving.
Hampshire police put a dispersal order in place and urged the public to avoid the area.
The government strongly condemned the protesters' intimidating and thuggish behaviour.
The asylum seekers were scheduled to be taken to Manston in Kent for processing.

title: Protesters clash with police after mega-dinghy arrives in Portsmouth
author: Charles Hymas; Keith Perry
content:
![Around 500 protesters are believed to have joined the demonstration in Portsmouth](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000501455854_17887280834360_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqf1s-wQoVbeXjDqs54TYD_tkM9MM8VM3G1BxlGUO4L8Q.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Around 500 protesters are believed to have joined the demonstration in Portsmouth](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000501455854_17887280834360_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqf1s-wQoVbeXjDqs54TYD_tkM9MM8VM3G1BxlGUO4L8Q.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Hundreds of protesters have clashed with police in Portsmouth after a mega-dinghy carrying 140 migrants reached the UK from Normandy.
Around 500 demonstrators are believed to have joined a protest in the area on Sunday night, with some dressed in all black – similar to those who joined an anti-illegal migrant protest which blocked the Port of Dover on Saturday.
The large boat of migrants – believed to be the longest-ever Channel crossing by people-smugglers – was intercepted in the Solent between the Isle of Wight and Portsmouth earlier on Sunday.
![Hundreds stage protest in Portsmouth after migrant boat arrives](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000501449769_17887264405260_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqRXuknvhZsb7bf88i7wdmgjZw8X5mnmN5SzvuuWR43vQ.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
![Police officers with riot shields form a line at the protest in Portsmouth](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000501456427_17887288364450_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqWZZ9520Qrn8RyVs0byqFf0R8YSybYNWDTYrGStsI8ko.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Demonstrators blocked the only access road to the marina in Eastney, where it is thought the migrants are being held.
Police used riot shields and pepper spray to force the crowds back, but the line broke through the weight of numbers. Protesters then made their way inside the marina compound.
Earlier, George Madgwick, the leader of Reform UK in Hampshire, wrote in a post on X that “over 100 migrant men” had arrived on the Portsmouth shore.
The French coastguard said it had detected the mega-dinghy, which was shadowed by a number of rescue boats in case it got into difficulties. Authorities estimated that up to 140 people were on board the vessel, 90 short of the record 230 who crossed on a similar boat last month.
At least 30 people were thrown off the boat into the sea because it was so overcrowded, according to French officials.
![Migrants are brought ashore from a lifeboat in Portsmouth](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000501452442_17887271916470_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqyuLFFzXshuGqnr8zPdDWXhbQKbwj1ZsnNMhuR7O6ySI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
It is understood that the boat’s occupants will be transferred to a facility in Manston, Kent, for processing, as is routine for small-boat arrivals in the area.
They were taken to shore in Portsmouth in two RNLI lifeboats after being rescued from a single dinghy south of the Isle of Wight in the English Channel.
Crews from Bembridge and Yarmouth on the Isle of Wight responded to reports of a small boat heading towards Hampshire.
One woman at the protest on Sunday, who did not want to give her name, said: “We want to stop them all coming in.
“We don’t need any more people in Hampshire.”
Another man, who gave his name as Matt, said: “People aren’t taking too kindly to it.”
![Hundreds of protesters descended on Portsmouth after a boat thought to be carrying asylum seekers sparked a major emergency response](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000501452355_17887272085671_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqyuLFFzXshuGqnr8zPdDWXhbQKbwj1ZsnNMhuR7O6ySI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
In a livestream from the scene, Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo – an associate of Right-wing activist Tommy Robinson – encouraged viewers to travel to Portsmouth to join the protest.
Thomas could be seen standing in the sea at the Eastney shingle beach, alongside a small group of other protesters, with police officers looking on.
“Roads are all blocked, they are never going to be able to leave here,” Thomas said.
He added: “It was only yesterday (at the protests in Dover) when we warned them that we will not accept this any more, and that this is no longer an option to tell us that the boat numbers are down.
“This isn’t about the numbers being down… this is about understanding that this has to come to an end now.”
The mega-dinghy – launched from a beach east of Cherbourg in the Baie de la Seine – reflects a change in tactics used by people-smugglers, who have started loading more migrants on to fewer and larger vessels, partly because of the success of law enforcement in disrupting boat and equipment supply chains.
As well as turning to larger boats, smuggling gangs have started launching taxi boats further west to avoid increased numbers of police on the beaches and to evade interception on the water by a new seaborne police unit.
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, said: “This week Andy Burnham struck an agreement for 45 more officers on French beaches.
“Today a boat launched from Baie de Seine, 170 miles from Calais, arriving on the beaches of Hampshire for the very first time. This is a joke. Only Reform will send the boats back.”
Joe Robertson, the Conservative MP for Isle of Wight East, posted: “Extremely concerning to see an illegal migrant crossing this far west.
“We don’t know if this migrant boat was headed for the Isle of Wight but I’ll be contacting the Home Office first thing. We need to know exactly what happened and if new routes are being used for mega-dinghies by people smugglers.”
A Hampshire Police spokesman said: “This evening, we have been working alongside and assisting our partners from Border Force, Maritime & Coastguard Agency and Portsmouth city council at Eastney Marina following the arrival of a boat crossing the Channel.
“We have officers in the area to ensure the prevention of any disorder. We ask that people please avoid the area. A dispersal order is in place until tomorrow evening (Monday, Sept 7). Anyone who refuses to comply with the direction to leave the area is liable for arrest.
“We can also confirm that Border Force has advised us that individuals will be transported outside of Hampshire for processing in the normal way after they have been safely disembarked.”
A Home Office spokesman said: “This Government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border. Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election.
“We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020.
“But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches.”
summary: Hundreds of protesters clashed with police in Portsmouth after a mega-dinghy carrying around 140 migrants arrived from Normandy, having been intercepted in the Solent. Demonstrators blocked access roads to the marina where the migrants were held, with crowds eventually breaking through police lines using weight of numbers. The incident highlights a shifting tactic by people-smugglers toward larger vessels launched further west.
key_points: Around 500 protesters demonstrated in Portsmouth on Sunday night following the arrival of a mega-dinghy carrying approximately 140 migrants.
Police used riot shields and pepper spray to hold back the crowds, but protesters broke through the line and entered the marina compound.
French officials reported that about 30 people were thrown off the overcrowded boat into the sea during the journey from Normandy.
Smugglers are shifting tactics toward larger vessels and launching from locations further west to evade law enforcement and police units.
The migrants are scheduled to be transferred to a facility in Manston, Kent, for routine processing.

title: Baby girl dies on camping trip in Staffordshire
author: Will Bolton
content:
![Staffordshire Police cordoned off a fishing lake close to the Wyrley and Essington Canal](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000500933971_17887077765620_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BquOv8qdqAtg5F-Rc30df4df4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Staffordshire Police cordoned off a fishing lake close to the Wyrley and Essington Canal](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000500933971_17887077765620_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BquOv8qdqAtg5F-Rc30df4df4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A three-month-old girl has died during a family camping trip in Staffordshire.
Police said their investigation into the “unexplained” death was in its early stages, describing it as an “isolated incident”.
Emergency services were called to a nature reserve off Strawberry Lane, near the village of Cheslyn Hay, at 8.45am on Saturday after a report of a child in cardiac arrest.
An air ambulance was sent to the scene, but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.
Officers cordoned off a fishing lake at the nature reserve, close to the Wyrley and Essington Canal. Drone images from the scene showed at least four tents and camping chairs next to each other, close to fishing platforms.
Det Insp Katie Gregory said: “While the investigation remains at an early stage, this is an isolated incident. The death is being treated as unexplained at this time.”
![Emergency services were called to a nature reserve off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, on Saturday morning](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/06/TELEMMGLPICT000500933924_17887078021510_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqZTGkdds8SWJRzcZ4ZecXrf4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The area is not an official camping site, but locals said teenagers often fished in two lakes there and camped overnight. A nearby nature trail is also popular with dog walkers and runners.
Robert Duncan, the South Staffordshire council district councillor for Cheslyn Hay, said: “I know how deeply upsetting news like this is for our community.
“It’s important that we allow the emergency services the space they need to complete their work with dignity and care.
“As soon as the full and confirmed details are formally shared with me, I will provide a further update to residents. Until then, please avoid speculation and allow the family and responders the privacy and respect they deserve.”
People living in Cheslyn Hay, which is three miles south of Cannock and has a population of about 7,000, left a floral tribute to the girl near to the scene.
Rev Samantha Hagerman, the superintendent of Cannock Chase Methodist Circuit, said: “Our thoughts and prayers are with family, friends and emergency services affected by the incident near Cheslyn Hay.”
summary: A three-month-old girl has died during a family camping trip at a nature reserve in Staffordshire. Emergency services responded to a report of a child in cardiac arrest, but she was pronounced dead at the scene. Staffordshire Police are currently treating the death as unexplained and described it as an isolated incident.
key_points: A three-month-old girl died during a family camping trip in Staffordshire.
Emergency services were called to a nature reserve off Strawberry Lane on Saturday morning.
Police and paramedics responded to a report of a child in cardiac arrest, but she was pronounced dead shortly after.
Authorities are treating the death as unexplained while the investigation remains in its early stages.

title: 140 migrants in single dinghy rescued in English Channel
author: Simon Jones; AndrÃ© Rhoden-Paul
content:
![Migrants on an inflatable dinghy leaving the coast of northern France at Gravelines, near Calais](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/5295/live/fa800b90-aa05-11f1-afb5-a367f96884d3.jpg)
Migrants on an inflatable dinghy near Calais in a separate attempt on Sunday
- Published
Around 140 migrants in a single dinghy have been rescued in the English Channel.
The people on the inflatable vessel, which launched from the Normandy coast overnight, requested help in UK waters and were picked up by two RNLI boats, the French coastguard said. They will now be taken to shore in the UK.
It comes days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings.
In August a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel.
The dinghy launched in Bay of the Seine and was shadowed for around 10 hours by French rescue boats in case it got into difficulty. The French coastguard said it was not safe to attempt to stop the dinghy on water.
It reached UK waters at lunchtime and the people on board were met by lifeboats from Bembridge and Yarmouth.
French authorities said it was unusual for the migrant boat to depart from the area - 170 miles away from the usual launches around Calais making the crossing to the UK significantly longer.
Last year local officials told the BBC there has been an increase in people trying to depart from Normandy.
A Home Office spokesperson said on Sunday: "This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border.
"Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election."
They added: "But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches."
In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.
While the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies".
It's thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area.
Between 1 January and 1 September 2026, a total of 16, 513 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France.
Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.
  - Published3 days ago
 ![A group of migrants on a dingy off the coast of Gravelines, in a grab from the BBC video.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/2bb1/live/cf1e6580-a764-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
- ![Large numbers of bright orange lifejackets are seen in plastic bags inside a warehouse](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/3113/live/6ce86220-9815-11f1-a7ea-19f04b81e9a0.png)
  - Published4 days ago
 ![A young person wearing a baseball cap and a backpack and carrying a suitcase stands in the middle of the image. To the left of the image a passport with a boarding card is held up. To the right of the image is a migrant family of a man, woman and child on a beach, walking. In the top right corner is a partial view of a UK visa document](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a530/live/da608860-cb5a-11f0-a892-01d657345866.png)
summary: Around 140 migrants in a single dinghy that launched from the Normandy coast were rescued in UK waters by RNLI boats. The unusual 170-mile journey comes amid increasing reports of smugglers using larger vessels to avoid detection following stricter policing near Calais. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron recently met to discuss scaling up efforts against small boat crossings.
key_points: About 140 migrants aboard a single inflatable dinghy were rescued by two RNLI boats after requesting help in UK waters.
The vessel launched from the Normandy coast, an unusual departure point that made the crossing significantly longer at 170 miles.
Smugglers are increasingly loading more people onto larger vessels, or 'mega dinghies', to avoid detection following robust policing in the Calais area.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron recently met to discuss scaling up joint efforts to reduce small boat crossings.

title: Farage says overseas donation row ‘looks bad’ but denies Reform broke law
author: Pippa Crerar
content:
Nigel Farage has acknowledged the overseas donation row engulfing Reform UK “looks bad” for his party but denied it had ever taken foreign money in breach of electoral law.
The Reform leader, who is battling to contain the fallout from the allegations, was asked if he could categorically rule out that foreign money had ever been funnelled to his party. He replied: “I can. Never happened.”
Farage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigation apparently plotting to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.
In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Farage described their comments as “injudicious at best” and admitted the optics of the undercover filming were problematic for his party, which has in the past tried to suggest it would do politics differently.
“This looks bad, as does the sale of peerages, as does government contracts for donations,” he said. “We are not the first people to be involved in a row over donations.”
The questions overshadowed the start of Reform’s party conference in Birmingham, where numerous hecklers were removed from the hall during Farage’s keynote speech.
Footage has emerged online of one of the women being dragged by her hair, with a man also appearing to hit female protesters with his crutch.
When questioned about the incident by Jon Sopel on Sky News’s Sunday Morning programme, Robert Jenrick said: “Oh, boohoo. We’re now in a country, Jon, where somebody who is – whatever she is – a far-left protester, goes into a party conference, tries to wreck the leader’s speech, and cries foul if a pensioner knocks her over the head with their Zimmer frame.
“I mean, come on, get a life,” Reform’s treasury spokesperson added.
West Midlands police said they were aware of the footage, adding: “We would ask the woman involved to come forward. Anyone with any information should contact us on 101 quoting log number 924 of 5 September.”
After an official complaint that Farage and his aides had broken political funding laws, the Metropolitan police said it was assessing the evidence, with sources suggesting a full investigation is expected. They all deny wrongdoing.
Scotland Yard could extend an existing investigation into whether Reform took donations channelled through an intermediary from potentially impermissible sources, which the party and donors deny.
Farage is already facing intense scrutiny about Reform’s finances, as well as about his £5m gift from a crypto billionaire shortly before he announced he would stand in the 2024 general election, which he has since said was intended to pay for security.
![Robert Jenrick speaks on stage during the party’s annual conference on Saturday](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/87fc83af710fca376c8fef43a7ccdc7e1a128925/0_0_5900_3933/master/5900.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In an earlier extract of the BBC interview, Farage also claimed he “wasn’t even listening” during the meeting at the centre of the controversy, and that he knew donation law “better than anybody”, as he sought to limit the damage caused by the allegations.
after newsletter promotion
Jenrick said on Sunday that he had seen legal advice that the party had not in fact broken electoral law over foreign donations but that lessons would be learned from the episode.
“We’re going to investigate exactly what happened,” Jenrick told Sky News. “It’s right to have due process. But this is not the way that Reform conducts itself.
“Like any political party, we seek to abide by the law at all times, and we believe we have in this case. In fact, I’ve reviewed the legal advice from the KC who’s advised the party in the last 48 hours, and it shows that, yeah, we did.
“But do we want for the best version of ourselves? Yes, absolutely. And no doubt there will be lessons to be learnt from this.”
Speaking after the BBC interview, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said: “For a political party that don’t like foreigners much, they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash. We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them.”
He added: “I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they’re really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going.”
summary: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has admitted that a row over alleged overseas donations looks bad for his party, though he denies breaking electoral law. The controversy stems from an undercover investigation that captured two senior aides apparently plotting to circumvent funding rules, prompting their suspension and a police assessment of the evidence. Meanwhile, the party's conference in Birmingham was disrupted by protesters, leading to police involvement regarding footage of physical altercations in the hall.
key_points: Nigel Farage denied Reform UK ever accepted foreign money in breach of electoral law, despite admitting the donation row looks bad.
Farage suspended two close aides, Dan Jukes and James Orr, after they were filmed apparently plotting to bypass laws on foreign donations.
The Metropolitan police are assessing evidence after an official complaint was made regarding political funding laws.
Reform conference speeches faced disruptions from protesters, with police reviewing online footage of physical altercations in the hall.

title: Police slow to respond to Dover protest, says council boss
author: Craig Buchan
content:
Masked men chanting "stop the boats" at Port of Dover
- Published
Police were slow to react to an "exceptionally well organised" protest that ground the Port of Dover to a halt for hours, a council boss has said.
Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, told the BBC that demonstrators "caught several agencies on the hoof" when they arrived on Saturday.
Hundreds of masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads, causing miles of tailbacks and preventing access to the port.
Kent Police is yet to comment, but cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds said officers "did deal with it swiftly".
Mills said the force "appeared to be quite slow to keep the roads and the networks open, which is disappointing".
"The protesters knew what they were doing, I'm not sure the police did know what was going to happen," he told the BBC.
"But then I accept that the police resource is stretched."
The Labour councillor said "no-one actually knew" what was happening on Saturday morning and there "needs to be a wash-up over that".
"All in all it was a pretty traumatic day for a lot of people travelling, trying to get around their business," he said.
Kent Police said on Saturday that officers made no arrests and described it as a "spontaneous protest".
Mills added that the council later received complaints from villagers in Preston, where "protesters appear to have parked their vehicles before they came in".
Chris Vinson, leader of the council's Conservative group, previously said the men had "loaded into rental vans" and then travelled to the town.
![Dozens of men dressed in black and wearing face coverings, being escorted down a dual carriageway in Dover by uniformed police officers.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/8b90/live/51566c00-a91d-11f1-a3dc-e78e2c02425d.jpg)
Hundreds of masked men blocked roads and prevented access to the Port of Dover
Reynolds, speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, condemned the protest.
"Peaceful protest is an essential part of British life but that is not what we saw there with that kind of intimidatory behaviour," the business secretary said.
"I feel sorry for the people around Dover and the people disrupted by that."
Police have not yet commented on who was behind the demonstration, which lasted from 07:00 BST to about 11:30.
Anti-hate organisation Hope Not Hate claimed the Patriot Platform network arranged it, saying the group began meeting in July and had brought together members of anti-migrant groups from around the country.
Demonstrators told the BBC they did not want to talk to the media, although one said "send them back" and another said "stop the boats" when approached on Saturday.
Far-right activists Tommy Robinson and Danny Thomas both posted about it on X, praising those involved.
Thomas wrote: "The experience on the ground today, was the overwhelming majority of the women and local people we spoke to were thankful that people were actually doing something."
He praised protesters for showing "discipline" and said they had "stuck to the plan".
Reynolds said that Robinson and others like him were "not interested in solving genuine problems this country has".
"They want to exploit their online following and take money from the people willing to follow them online, and that's what that agenda is," he said.
"This government is about solving the problems that really make a difference to people's lives."
Great Yarmouth MP and leader of Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe, said his party "proudly stands with those peacefully protesting against illegal immigration in Dover".
In a video on X, he said wearing balaclavas was "undesirable" but "perfectly fair for people living in this Orwellian age".
Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.
summary: Hundreds of masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads and ground the Port of Dover to a halt for several hours on Saturday. Dover District Council leader Kevin Mills criticized Kent Police for being slow to respond to the well-organised demonstration, though cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds argued officers dealt with it swiftly. Kent Police initially described the event as a spontaneous protest and made no arrests. Meanwhile, anti-hate organisation Hope Not Hate attributed the arrangement to the Patriot Platform network.
key_points: Hundreds of masked protesters blocked roads and access to the Port of Dover on Saturday.
Council leader Kevin Mills stated that police were slow to respond and keep networks open.
Cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds condemned the protest's intimidatory behaviour.
Kent Police described the event as a spontaneous protest and made no arrests.
Hope Not Hate claimed the Patriot Platform network organised the demonstration.

title: Nigel Farage denies wrongdoing over foreign donor talks on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg
author: Live Reporting Edited by Alex Smith
content:
![Laura Kuenssberg interviews Nigel Farage](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/9/6/cf05bf4c-0a97-494a-b841-82643f9f60f8.jpg.webp)
This week's show has just finished - here's a recap of what we heard:
Nigel Farage
In a pre-recorded interview, the Reform UK leader told Laura Kuenssberg he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK - more on that in our previous post.
He is also asked about a proposed Reform policy that, if the party was in government, would see the threshold before people pay income tax increased to Â£15,000.
Asked how the party would pay for it, Farage says: "We are taking benefits away from foreign nationals and social housing away from foreign nationals and from some Brits we donât think should qualify and we canât afford.â
Jonathan Reynolds
On the Reform foreign donor story, the business secretary says: âWe have rules in this country, about how our democracy works, and everyone has to stick to them.â
Reynolds also condemned a protest by masked 'stop the boats' demonstrators in Dover on Saturday, which blocked traffic from entering and leaving the port for hours.
Andrew Griffith
The newly-appointed shadow chancellor talks about the state of the public finances, saying the government is "signing up to more and more debt to our children".
He says any future government would have to "take difficult decisions" to get the country growing.
We're ending our live coverage. You can watch back the episode in full in the watch & listen tab at the top of the page - and read Laura Kuenssberg's write-up of her Farage interview here.
summary: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage denied wrongdoing in an interview with Laura Kuenssberg regarding discussions about funneled foreign money, stating he was not listening during the conversation. Farage also explained that a proposed income tax threshold increase to £15,000 would be funded by removing benefits and social housing from foreign nationals and certain British citizens. Meanwhile, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds emphasized the importance of following democracy rules and condemned a Dover protest, while Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith discussed public finances and national debt.
key_points: Nigel Farage denied wrongdoing over talks involving potential foreign funding for Reform UK.
Farage proposed raising the income tax threshold to £15,000 by cutting benefits and social housing for foreign nationals and ineligible Brits.
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds stated that everyone must adhere to UK democracy rules.
Reynolds condemned a masked 'stop the boats' protest in Dover that blocked port traffic.
Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith warned about increasing national debt and the need for difficult economic decisions.

title: Chancellor warns of tough Budget as Iran war puts strain on economy
author: Maryam Zakir-Hussain
content:
The upcoming autumn Budget is expected to be tough, the chancellor has warned, as the US-Iran war continues to damage the economy.
John Healey issued the warning following a leap in government borrowing earlier this week, reflecting concerns among lenders about the inflationary impact of Donald Trump’s war with Iran.
However, Mr Healey also told the Financial Times he would ensure the UK emerges from his first Budget, on 28 October, with a solid “buffer against uncertainty”.
The chancellor told the FT: “What’s happening in the Middle East is hitting inflation, it’s hitting growth, it’s hitting borrowing costs.”
He added: “It’s part of a more dangerous world that is more uncertain and it’s one of the challenges we have to meet in this country, but have to meet with other [countries].”
![Chancellor John Healey warns the autumn Budget will be tough](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/07/aeb88c87603ecee43892dd7897d3d44fY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MjA3NzA2-2.85365880.jpg)
Economists have predicted that the fiscal buffer Rachel Reeves built up in her last Budget, through a combination of tax rises and departmental spending cuts, will be squeezed by the inflationary pressures of ongoing global turmoil.
This could limit Andy Burnham’s ambitions to tackle the cost of living crisis, and spending plans across his wider agenda for government.
Mr Healey declined to tell the newspaper how much fiscal headroom he planned to maintain above his spending plans after the Budget.
A key fiscal rule requires the Treasury to bring the Budget into surplus by the end of the parliament, excluding investment.
He told the newspaper that both he and the prime minister were “in lockstep in our determination to meet the fiscal rules” and added that it would be achieved “with a buffer against the sort of uncertainty that we have talked about”.
![Donald Trump’s war with Iran is putting strain on the UK economy](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/04/20/2026-09-04T193216Z_1523549726_RC2JCNAF4UTJ_RTRMADP_3_USA-TRUMP.JPG)
Mr Healey has come under fire from the Conservatives for not recommitting to spending 3 per cent of GDP on defence by 2030.
When he resigned as Sir Keir Starmer’s defence secretary, he suggested hitting this target was vital to keep the country safe.
He did however tell the FT that the UK would hit its goal of raising defence spending to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2035, a Nato commitment, but said this would be set out at next year’s spending review.
The chancellor has also announced changes to Treasury rules aimed at helping to speed up regional regeneration across the country.
A major change to the Treasury’s green book, its guide to evaluating the costs and benefits of government projects and programmes, will be to lower something called the “discount rate”.
Reducing this from 3.5 per cent to 3 per cent will make it easier to demonstrate the long-term value of spending public money on building new schools and roads, among other projects.
The announcement comes ahead of a major speech on the economy Mr Healey is due to make on Monday.
Additional reporting from Press Association.
summary: Chancellor John Healey has warned that the upcoming autumn Budget will be difficult due to economic pressures from the US-Iran war. He emphasized that the UK must build a solid fiscal buffer against uncertainty while meeting established fiscal rules. Additionally, the Treasury announced changes to its evaluation rules to help speed up regional regeneration projects.
key_points: The upcoming autumn Budget is expected to be tough due to the economic impact of the US-Iran war.
Chancellor John Healey stated that the situation in the Middle East is negatively affecting inflation, growth, and borrowing costs.
The UK remains committed to meeting fiscal rules and maintaining a buffer against uncertainty.
Treasury rules are changing to lower the discount rate from 3.5 per cent to 3 per cent to support regional regeneration projects.

title: Major disruption as grass fire hits Heathrow train links
author: Ewan Somerville
content:
![Crowds fill the concourse of London Paddington station with the departure boards blank showing no services.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/de80/live/5ff9eda0-a962-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Departure boards appeared to have gone blank at Paddington as train services were cut into Saturday evening
- Published
Trains to and from Heathrow Airport have been halted after a trackside grass fire caused delays and cancellations.
National Rail said "major disruption" was expected until the end of Saturday following the incident which began shortly after 16:00 BST.
A statement said all lines were blocked between London Paddington station and Heathrow's terminals, as well as Reading, due to "a failure of the electricity supply caused by a fire next to the track".
It comes hours after a separate grass fire on Heathrow's airfield shut a runway earlier on Saturday.
Pictures on social media showed crowds of stranded passengers at Paddington, one of London's main rail hubs.
London Fire Brigade said six fire engines and around 40 crew members were tackling the blaze near Scrubs Lane, North Kensington.
Great Western Railway, external cancelled its services to Reading and no Elizabeth line or Heathrow Express services were running between Paddington and Heathrow on Saturday night.
The airport advised passengers to leave extra time for their journeys, adding that the Piccadilly line, which runs services to the airport, also has delays.
Earlier on Saturday, Heathrow's southern runway was closed while crews tackled a grass fire on the airfield.
It caused some disruption with at least two flights diverted elsewhere. Heathrow apologised for any disruption and said the fire was extinguished quickly.
That comes weeks after another grass fire near Heathrow's southern runway which forced 18 flights to divert and destroyed a large area of grassland.
While weather has cooled across much of the UK in recent days following record-breaking heat over the summer, fire crews have still been warning of wildfire risks.
The Met Office's Fire Severity Index, external shows that if a wildfire was to occur, it would have a "high" fire severity in most of south-east England and some of the Midlands.
The fire severity is "exceptional", the highest level on the index, in some parts of London including Heathrow, as well as on the Essex and Suffolk coasts.
- ![Part suspended service information board at station](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/f886/live/d55e47c0-94a0-11f1-b485-c780285c5cc1.jpg)
  - Published31 July
 ![A composite of a Heathrow fire and rescue truck on a runway and Edward Killiwick](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a427/live/adfea090-8cde-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
- ![Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/f13c/live/382364b0-679f-11f0-8979-21e9e3d3b0da.png)
- ![A woman uses an umbrella to shelter from the sun, surrounded by several other people, in a sun-drenched Trafalgar Square in London](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/84de/live/4bd31cb0-a51c-11f1-89d5-dd5482a9fcc2.jpg)
summary: A trackside grass fire near Scrubs Lane caused major disruptions and electricity supply failures, halting train services between London Paddington, Heathrow Airport, and Reading. National Rail warned that the disruptions would last until the end of Saturday, leaving crowds of passengers stranded. This incident followed an earlier grass fire on Heathrow's airfield that temporarily closed a runway and forced flight diversions.
key_points: Trains between London Paddington, Heathrow Airport, and Reading were halted due to an electricity supply failure caused by a trackside grass fire.
Major disruption was expected to continue through the end of Saturday, affecting Great Western Railway, Elizabeth line, and Heathrow Express services.
London Fire Brigade deployed six fire engines and about 40 crew members to tackle the blaze near Scrubs Lane in North Kensington.
A separate grass fire earlier on Saturday closed Heathrow's southern runway and led to flight diversions.
The Met Office's Fire Severity Index rated wildfire risk as exceptional in parts of London, including Heathrow.

title: ‘I wasn’t even listening,’ Farage says of donations scandal meeting
author: Ben Quinn; Peter Walker
content:
Nigel Farage has claimed that he “wasn’t even listening” during a meeting at the centre of a controversy about whether his party considered evading the law on accepting donations from overseas.
The Reform UK leader also claimed he knew donation law “better than anybody” during interviews as he sought to salvage the final day of his party conference from the fallout that has already cost him two of his closest aides.
Farage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigation appearing to plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.
The undercover reporters from a group called Verbatim posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party when it was published in national newspapers.
The Reform leader himself remains under pressure over a separate clip in which he was heard saying “it’s all above board” after one of the reporters who was posing as the UK-based son of a wealthy US backer told Farage he had been in discussions with Jukes and Orr for some time.
“I’ll be the registered donor,” the son says. “But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that’s done and all those conversations are had the money is available.”
In an interview on Saturday, Farage told the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg that “of course” he knew it was illegal for foreign firms to donate to UK parties, adding he was told the money was being given via a UK family office.
When challenged by Kuenssberg that while in Farage’s presence, one of the undercover reporters had said they “run an American family office”, the Reform leader said: “I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton byelection. I turn up. I frankly wasn’t even listening.”
He added: “I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore. The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have come from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.”
Farage’s party had been hoping to move the focus to policy announcements, including on tax cuts, as Reform’s conference closed in Birmingham on Saturday.
![Reform MP Robert Jenrick addresses the conference](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9b99afd04b49474e56b6a1cbc60bb9777a0197ac/2568_926_1495_1753/master/1495.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Its Treasury spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, gave a keynote speech in which he pledged to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 within the first 100 days if the party were to take office. The threshold has been set at £12,570 since 2021 and is due to remain there until 2031.
But in interviews given earlier in the day to trail the policy, he also found himself forced to deflect from the donations controversy. “That’s been dealt with,” he told GB News. “The two individuals concerned have gone, and we’re here today moving forward. The language that they used was clearly inappropriate, that was very disappointing.”
In an interview with Times Radio he said Orr and Jukes had been “permanently suspended”, appearing to differ from the latest party line that they had “stepped down pending outcome of an investigation”, indicating a possible way back.
Farage meanwhile accused “the establishment” of trying to derail Reform UK, when challenged by ITV’s Robert Peston on the string of allegations related to his and the party’s finances.
“And it will go on. You come back and see me in six months, there’ll be five more investigations. It won’t end. This won’t end,” he said.
Farage said he had some “thoughtful” moments over the summer, claiming his family had been asking him to “walk away” from politics amid pressure on them and him.
Despite Reform’s efforts to insulate Farage, the Met police are now assessing evidence after a complaint that the Reform leader, as well as Orr and Jukes, may have broken political funding laws. They all deny wrongdoing.
after newsletter promotion
The final day of the conference also coincided with an appeal by West Midlands police for a woman, who was among climate activists who were removed from the hall on Friday as they heckled Farage’s speech, to come forward after footage emerged over her allegedly being assaulted.
The police initially responded on X to a clip that appeared to show audience members pulling her hair and grabbing her head as she was carried out of the conference hall. West Midlands police later said in a statement that they were aware of a video circulating from the Reform UK conference showing an incident with a protester, and had asked the woman to come forward.
The activist group Climate Resistance, which claimed responsibility for the protest during Farage’s speech , said the protester was considering whether to speak to police.
![A woman raising her fist into the air as she’s being carried out by a number of men](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/15c4bf306d28ffe62d61001df5675473a9c54ea3/0_0_6540_4362/master/6540.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Nadine Dorries, a former Conservative MP who has joined Reform, said sensitivities were “heightened” in the aftermath of the killing of the Reform spokesperson Ann Widdecombe in July.
“They tried to completely derail the speech. It was an organised sting again,” she said in an interview with LBC when asked about the incident.
Also speaking on Saturday was Suella Braverman, the party’s education spokesperson who, like Jenrick, is another defector from the Conservatives.
Her speech announced a planned cut of 20% to the number of student loans given, with funds only granted to university courses that can demonstrate good economic returns, with exceptions for some courses “of strategic or cultural importance”.
![Nigel Farage standing at the podium in his pastel turquoise suit with his arms spread in front of other Reform representatives](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1544f3e13387a944bf5591cb5c49e7881332f5f1/0_0_8640_5760/master/8640.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Farage ended the conference with closing comments to the main hall, where sections of seating were unoccupied and the mood was more subdued than earlier in the event, by telling the Reform faithful that “there would be good days and bad days”.
“Sometimes we will get things wrong and get a bit of a kicking, but what this conference has shown is that whatever you throw at the leadership, whatever you throw at you, the people’s army, we immediately stop, pick ourselves up and start all over again,” he said.
summary: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage defended himself over a donations scandal on the final day of his party's conference, claiming he "wasn't even listening" during a meeting where aides were filmed appearing to plot around electoral laws. The controversy forced the suspension of two close aides and overshadowed policy announcements, including proposed tax cuts and higher education funding changes. Meanwhile, the Metropolitan Police are assessing evidence regarding potential political funding law violations, which Farage and his suspended aides deny.
key_points: Nigel Farage claimed he was not listening during a meeting where two Reform aides were filmed appearing to plot to bypass electoral laws on foreign donations.
Farage suspended aide Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr following an undercover investigation by Verbatim.
The Metropolitan Police are assessing evidence after a complaint that Farage, Jukes, and Orr may have broken political funding laws, though all deny wrongdoing.
The party conference also featured policy pledges, including Robert Jenrick's proposal to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000.
West Midlands police appealed for a female climate activist to come forward after footage emerged of her allegedly being assaulted while being removed from the conference hall.

title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks
author: Laura Kuenssberg
content:
Watch: The Reform UK leader says he "frankly wasnât even listening" during a conversation about foreign money being donated to his party
- Published
Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.
His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.
Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.
In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.
In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News, Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives Â£500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.
Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.
The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.
When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board.
In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening."
"I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film.
![A shot of Dan Jukes and Nigel Farage in the Channel 4 News report.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/49ae/live/87b69b70-a92d-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Undercover reporters posing as party donors met with Nigel Farage and his former chief of staff Dan Jukes (left)
"The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.
"Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."
The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate.
Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.
Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.
But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics.
"They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said.
He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy".
Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.
Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations.
He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."
Analysis: Farage may have to pay more attention
![Laura Kuenssberg looks at the camera in a red jacket, in front of light blue Reform banners and a light blue carpet.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/79b1/live/409512d0-a92d-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Laura Kuenssberg has been speaking to senior Reform figures and members at the party's annual conference in Birmingham
There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.
Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".
They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.
They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.
They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.
Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.
But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.
What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.
At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.
One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".
No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".
And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.
Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.
A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up â sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".
Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.
But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera â Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."
But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"
This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.
Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling â to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.
summary: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage stated that he "wasn't listening" during a recorded conversation involving his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing a potential foreign donation scheme. The controversy led to the removal of two senior staff members and prompted calls from political opponents for a police investigation. Farage also revealed that mounting political pressure has caused his family to beg him to leave politics.
key_points: Nigel Farage claimed he was not listening during a conversation about funneling foreign money to Reform UK recorded in an undercover film.
Former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr were removed from their roles pending an internal investigation.
The Metropolitan Police are assessing whether to investigate the claims following calls from Labour and the Liberal Democrats.
Farage stated that his family is begging him to leave his job due to increasing pressure.
Farage also condemned masked protesters who caused travel disruption at the Port of Dover.

title: Black-clad protesters in balaclavas block road at port of Dover in Kent
author: Donna Ferguson; Priya Bharadia
content:
Dozens of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road at the port of Dover in Kent, forcing closures in both directions on Saturday morning.
Kent police said they were were in attendance and engaging with the protest, which the Port of Dover described as a “public order incident”. No arrests were made during the incident. Responsibility for the demonstration appears to have been claimed by an anti-immigration group with links to the far right.
The behaviour of the participants and the travel disruption they have caused has been condemned by the government. Traffic in and out of the port on the A20 was stopped, causing delays of up to 30 minutes and four miles of congestion, according to National Highways.
Videos and pictures shared online showed a large number of masked people in black marching on the road in a large group as lorries waited in traffic next to police cars.
By Saturday lunchtime, the protesters had dispersed and access roads to the port were “free flowing”, according to the Port of Dover. Ferry operators pledged to put those who had been delayed by the disruption on to the next available sailings.
![Masked people on the road in Dover.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/70cd1ddff7221708adb05e3140dcbd192bdb8d0f/210_0_2584_1882/master/2584.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The number of people involved was not yet clear. One of those livestreaming the event estimated he was marching alongside hundreds of people. The Press Association reported that there were dozens in attendance but police have not given an official estimate.
Videos circulating on social media showed demonstrators linking arms in a blockade across the A20 and shouting “stop the boats”. They could be seen marching along the A road, chanting: “England till I die.”
A group called Patriot Platform, which styles itself as having “a fierce love for our homeland”, appeared to claim responsibility for the blockade on social media.
The far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, reposted multiple videos of the blockade, highlighting a live stream of the protest that directed viewers towards Patriot Platform.
In his post, Robinson encouraged more to join, saying “get there to support them”.
In another post, he wrote: “Simultaneously at different locations across Dover patriots have mobilised to close down the port. There are 3 plus locations that patriots have shut down so far with many more planned to be closed. People wanted action I’m guessing there are 100,000’s of men willing to fill their shoes.”
The founder of Patriot Platform, Danny Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, wrote on social media “live Dover somethings [sic] happening” and posted a live stream.
In a video posted on 2 September, he told his followers he was meeting with “a huge group [of] top, proper patriots” to prepare for a message he was planning to send to the government. 
 “Very, very soon, we are going to send a message that will make sure they understand that we will not go down without a fight. We will not allow our nation to be plagued in the way that it is. And when you see it and when you feel it, I guarantee the whole thing will change for the better. Because once the message is sent once, imagine the sheer numbers that will be sent on the second, the third, the fourth message.”
In further comments, he said: “From the hills of Scotland to the fields of Wales to the streets of Northern Ireland and to the towns and cities of England, we are building something that’s never been built before. And when you’re part of it and you see what’s about to go down, you will understand … we’re about to show you what can be done when men and women of this country, who have the blood that runs through them like their grandfathers, get off their asses and do something about it.”
![Dozens of balaclava-wearing protesters stand in the road](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/73ece0d276f0654f5f24bd5827e4d6a78a01093b/276_0_2567_1652/master/2567.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
On Saturday morning, the Port of Dover confirmed in a statement that the disruption was affecting “all routes” in and out, as well as around the town, and that it was in touch with the police.
It said: “The Port of Dover can confirm that there is an ongoing public order incident happening around the town of Dover. This situation is impacting our local community and our customers, so of course we are hoping for a swift resolution.”
Nathan Ditchburn, who was on his way to work when he saw the group arrive at about 6.45am, told KentOnline: “I would say there are around 300 men, maybe more. Nobody will speak; they just handed me a piece of paper to look at. They have blocked off every entrance and exit of the Dover port area, and Jubilee Way is blocked as well. It will be causing huge delays for the ferries today.”
The local parkrun group cancelled its Dover Waterfront run, telling runners the course was unsafe or blocked. A spokesperson told KentOnline: “I am afraid we are going to cancel this morning. We have mass disruption with some protesters.”
Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and Deal, criticised what he described as “idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption”. In a post on Facebook, he said: “Parkrun cancelled and port access disrupted. I am fed up with idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption. I bet if you asked any one of those ‘protesters’ they wouldn’t know small boat crossings are down by 40% and we are working hard to fix the mess. Go home, enjoy your weekend/get a job.”
Chris Vinson, the leader of the Conservative group on Dover district council, said the protest appeared to be “illegal migration-related”, but said the demonstrators did not appear to have placards or banners.
“I’m not aware that there’s been any violence, although clearly, having the path of your vehicle blocked by men wearing black paramilitary gear and balaclavas is extremely intimidating, especially when it’s not clear why they’re there, and the police weren’t aware and so haven’t been able to warn people in advance and make sure that they are made to feel safe,” he said.
“I know people who have worked night shifts in the port who are being prevented from leaving for fears for their safety.”
A local Reform UK councillor, Paul King, told residents to avoid the port area. “I’ve been told it’s a stop the boats protest.” he said.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused. We appreciate the frustration of those who have been impacted today. Access to the port is now restored and traffic is flowing. Those travelling to the Port are advised to allow for extra travel time and to follow guidance from providers.
“We thank policing partners and travel providers who we continue to work with to ensure the safety of passengers and the wider community.”
The shipping company DFDS said: “We are aware of the current traffic disruption affecting access to the port. Rest assured we will accommodate you on to the next departure once you arrive.”
P&O Ferries said its sailings were still going ahead as scheduled, adding that those who missed their departure would be offered the next available crossing.
summary: Dozens of black-clad protesters wearing balaclavas blocked roads at the port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing travel disruptions and delays. The demonstration, linked by reports and social media to an anti-immigration group called Patriot Platform, was condemned by the government and local officials. By Saturday lunchtime, police and port authorities confirmed the protesters had dispersed and access roads were free-flowing.
key_points: Protesters dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked roads in both directions at the port of Dover on Saturday morning.
The demonstration caused up to 30-minute delays and four miles of congestion on the A20 before roads were cleared by lunchtime.
Responsibility for the blockade appeared to be claimed by an anti-immigration group named Patriot Platform.
The government, local politicians, and the Port of Dover condemned the disruption and the behavior of the participants.
No arrests were made during the incident, and ferry operators accommodated delayed passengers on subsequent sailings.

title: ‘Winds of change’: How Milei is stirring Falklands claim amid Trump-UK spat
author: Caolán Magee
content:
![DAVOS, SWITZERLAND - JANUARY 22: U.S. President Donald Trump shakes hands with President of Argentina Javier Milei during a signing ceremony for the “Board of Peace” at the World Economic Forum (WEF) on January 22, 2026 in Davos, Switzerland. The US-backed “Board of Peace” is intended to administer the fragile ceasefire in the Gaza Strip after the war between Israel and Hamas. The final makeup of the board has not been confirmed. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/getty_6a9abfc902-1788526537.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Argentina’s President Javier Milei is capitalising on his country’s long-running claim to the Falkland Islands by coupling threats of sanctions over a major offshore oil project with lavish praise for Donald Trump, after the US president publicly questioned Washington’s position over the disputed UK territory.
Milei’s remarks come as relations between Trump and the UK government have deteriorated over the UK’s refusal to support US military action against Iran, and as the right-wing Milei increasingly positions Argentina as one of Washington’s closest ideological allies in Latin America.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Israel takes its war on Palestine into the AI age
- list 2 of 4‘Build The Wall’: White House arcade games face backlash
- list 3 of 4Reform UK officials step down as new funding scandal hits far-right party
- list 4 of 4India’s Smriti Mandhana becomes top run-scorer in women’s cricket
The UK has administered the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls Las Malvinas, since 1833. However, as the islands lie off its shores, Argentina claims sovereignty over them.
The US has traditionally supported the UK’s claim to the territory. But analysts say Trump’s willingness to question established US policy, even if mainly intended as leverage against London, could provide Milei with an opportunity to unite Argentinians around one of the country’s few enduring national causes.
The question of Argentina’s claim to the islands was raised again this week when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s son, Yair, accused the UK of hypocrisy and wrote on X in Spanish: “The Falkland Islands belong to Argentina.”
Here’s what we know.
What is the dispute over the Falkland Islands?
The Falklands are a self-governing British overseas territory in the South Atlantic, almost 13,000km (8,000 miles) from the UK.
Argentina says it inherited sovereignty over the islands from Spain in the 19th century. But Britain has administered the Falklands since 1833 and points both to that long presence and to the wishes of the islanders living there to justify its control. In a 2013 referendum, 1,513 of 1,517 voters backed remaining a British overseas territory.
The dispute erupted into war in 1982 when Argentina seized the islands.
The UK, under then-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, sent a military force to retake the territory, with 74 days of fighting left 649 Argentine and 255 British service members dead.
What has Milei said now?
In a nationally televised speech on Thursday, Milei seized on Trump’s suggestion that Washington might reconsider its position on the islands, and heralded the “winds of change” he said were blowing in favour of Argentina’s claim to the Falkland Islands.
“The United States is considering this change in position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” Milei said.
He also announced measures aimed at obstructing development of the Sea Lion oil project, about 220km (140 miles) north of the islands. The Sea Lion field sits in waters administered by the Falklands, and Argentina considers the project an illegal exploitation of resources in waters it claims as its own.
Rockhopper Exploration, a UK-based oil and gas exploration and production company with interests in the Falkland Islands, and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum are set to begin drilling in the coming months, with oil production expected to begin in 2028.
Milei also threatened tougher sanctions against companies involved in the project and announced new funding for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego, Argentina’s southernmost province, to strengthen the country’s military presence near the islands.
“Argentina will not stand idly by,” he said. “Any further advance on the Malvinas Islands will be considered a violation of our national security.”
“We can argue about my style. We can disagree over fiscal or exchange-rate policy,” Milei added. “But there are causes that rise above any political difference. The Malvinas is one of them.”
Why have Trump’s comments caused concern in Britain?
Trump has stopped short of outright endorsing Argentina’s claim to the islands, but he has repeatedly raised the possibility that Washington’s position on the islands could change.
In an interview with the right-wing GB News in the UK this week, Trump appeared to suggest he might not come to the UK’s aid if a conflict erupts with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.
He said the UK “was not there to help me” with the war with Iran.
“We didn’t need help, but I did ask NATO, and I asked your former leader, ‘Why didn’t you send a couple of ships?'”
Asked separately by the BBC if the longstanding US position on the UK’s claim to the Falklands was under review, Trump said: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.”
Trump’s comments followed reports that US defence officials were considering using Washington’s position on the Falklands as leverage to pressure the UK to increase military spending, including the possibility of opposing UK sovereignty over the islands.
The idea has been around for some time. In April, a leaked Pentagon email proposed reviewing US support for the UK’s position on the Falklands as a way to pressure London over its refusal to support US military action against Iran.
Christoph Bluth, a professor at the University of Bradford in the UK, told Al Jazeera that the context is crucial.
“Trump has not endorsed Argentina’s sovereignty claim; he has merely said the US position is under review,” Bluth said.
He added that the idea appeared to have originated “inside the Pentagon as leverage against Britain over defence spending and its refusal to support US action against Iran, not from a reassessment of the Falklands dispute itself”.
How has the UK responded to all this?
The UK has reiterated its position. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the UK’s commitment to the islands was “unshakeable”, while a spokesperson for Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the islanders had a right to determine their own future and that the UK’s commitment was “unwavering”.
Matthew Benwell, a specialist on the Falklands and geopolitics, told Al Jazeera that Trump’s comments would cause unease in both London and Stanley, the Falklands capital, but cautioned against viewing them as a policy change.
“At this stage, these are just remarks from President Trump,” he said. Whether they lead to a change in the US sovereignty position or an explicit call for negotiations “remains to be seen”, he said, adding that such a shift looked unlikely for now.
How can Milei make this situation work in his favour?
Washington has historically recognised the UK’s de facto administration of the islands without formally taking a position on sovereignty.
That neutrality has mattered to London. Klaus Dodds, a professor at Royal Holloway, University of London, told Al Jazeera that the UK has traditionally been able to rely on having a closer relationship with Washington than Argentina does.
“Now that has changed,” he said. With Trump still in office and closely aligned with Milei, Dodds said the Argentinian president is likely to view the moment as an opportunity “to take advantage whenever and wherever he can”.
Milei has appeared repeatedly at pro-Trump events in the US, attended his second inauguration and been called Trump’s “favourite president”.
Last year, Trump authorised a $20bn financial lifeline package for Argentina, tying support to Milei’s party succeeding in legislative elections. After his La Libertad Avanza party won, Trump authorised additional imports of Argentinian beef to the US.
Eleonora Natale, an analyst focusing on Latin American politics, said any US openness towards Argentina on the Falklands had to be seen within that wider relationship.
“Milei has become one of Trump’s closest ideological allies in Latin America,” she told Al Jazeera, pointing to shared positions on security, migration and scepticism towards multilateral institutions.
Tilmann Altenberg, a reader in Hispanic Studies at Cardiff University, also cautioned against interpreting Trump’s remarks as a settled shift over sovereignty.
His comments, Altenberg said, were “first and foremost a reflection on the relationship between the US and the UK, rather than a deliberate shift in US policy” towards the islands.
But he said Milei may nevertheless see the current alignment as “a window of opportunity” to advance Argentina’s position and strengthen his hand ahead of the 2027 election.
Could US support actually affect the dispute?
Analysts said a genuine change in Washington’s position would be significant, but its practical effects would be limited.
Dodds said abandoning neutrality would mark a break with a “fundamental tenet of US policy post-1982” and could be read as Trump rewarding Milei while punishing the UK for refusing to support US operations against Iran.
Bluth said US backing could give Argentina greater international leverage and make companies more cautious about investing in oil projects around the Falklands.
But, he added, it “would not be a material change or oblige Britain to negotiate sovereignty”.
Buenos Aires cannot physically prevent production at the Sea Lion oil field, Bluth added, but it can use sanctions and legal pressure against companies involved in developing it.
Trump’s remarks may also have symbolic value in Argentina even before any formal US decision, Altenberg added. In Buenos Aires they “might be perceived as a sign that the sovereignty question could be tabled before the international community again soon”, he said.
summary: Argentine President Javier Milei is leveraging his close ideological alliance with US President Donald Trump and recent tensions between Washington and London to press Argentina's sovereignty claim over the Falkland Islands. Trump has publicly questioned long-standing US policy regarding the UK-administered territory, serving as potential leverage over British defense policies and the UK's refusal to support US action against Iran. In response, Milei has announced measures to obstruct the Sea Lion offshore oil project, threatened sanctions against involved companies, and sought to strengthen Argentina's military presence.
